results.content:
Practical next step Turn this guide into a usable AI workflow Use short Coursiv lessons to practice the exact AI habits behind this topic. Start practicing

If you feel left behind by AI, take a breath — you are not in a race you have already lost. AI moves fast, but most people are earlier than the hype suggests. Start small: learn a few basics, try one tool on a real task, and build from there. Curiosity, not panic, is what closes the gap. [...] A sensible starting kit looks like this. Use one free AI assistant as your daily practice ground. Add a beginner-friendly guide or short course for structure, so you are not guessing what to learn next. Follow one reliable source to stay informed without drowning in hype. And find one community where you can ask beginner questions without embarrassment — seeing others learn openly is reassuring and speeds you up. If you want a guided, structured path rather than piecing it together alone, Explore Coursiv AI lessons offers short, applied lessons focused on using AI on real tasks. [...] Learn the basics. Spend a little time understanding what AI is and, roughly, how today’s tools work. A basic mental model removes most of the mystery.
 Find your starting point. Be honest about what you already know. You are probably further along than you feel, and knowing your level tells you where to begin.
 Connect it to your world. Look at how AI applies to your field or daily tasks. Relevance turns abstract learning into something useful.
 Practice on a real task. Pick one thing you actually need to do and try an AI tool on it. Doing beats watching every time.
 Build the habit. Use AI a little, regularly, rather than cramming once. Small, repeated contact is what makes it stick.

results.title: Feeling Behind on AI? Here's What Actually Helps. – Avi Hakhamanesh
results.content:
Most people stop at set up.

But the real leverage is treating these as living systems you keep refining.

Once you’ve built a Project or GPT, don’t just leave it. Pay attention to how it performs each time you use it, and keep improving it.

There are two separate levers:

1. Refine your instructions

   Both Projects and GPTs have a place for instructions—the prompt that tells AI the process to follow and how to respond each time.

   If you’re constantly correcting the same things (the formatting or tone is off, it’s too long or short, it skips a step), that’s a signal.

   Figure out what’s not working and update your instructions to be more specific. The goal is better results on the first try.
2. Add context documents (the “mini bibles” part) [...] 1. Focus on learning the next generation of tools like Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex which are far more powerful, but have a much steeper learning curve (this will be my #1 priority)

2. Explore something I’m increasingly convinced is urgently needed: There’s a growing gap between what you need to actually learn this technology and what exists to help and support you to get there.

Even the steps I laid out in this edition—Projects, GPTs, context documents—I know they’re hard to do alone.

Especially when you’re trying to figure it all out at 11pm after a full day of work, parenting, and everything else life throws at you.

And we’re about to hit another inflection point. [...] Project context. The backstory on what you’re working on. Who the stakeholders are. Political dynamics or sensitivities. Constraints you’re operating within. The stuff that lives in your head but the AI has no way of knowing.
 Examples of good work. If you’re creating proposals, upload a few that landed well. If you’re writing social media posts, include examples of your highest-performing ones and explain why they worked. Showing the AI what “good” looks like for you is one of the fastest ways to improve results.
 Audience profiles. Not a one-liner, but real detail. Who they are, what they care about, what motivates them, what turns them off, what problems they’re trying to solve, any other psychographics that help AI better understand them.

# If You Feel Behind On AI, Read This

Stop Trying to Learn AI. Start Using It.

Alexis Haselberger

6 Min Read

## TL/DR:

 You’re never going to “learn AI” as a subject. It’s too big and moves too fast. Stop trying.
 Instead, learn WITH AI by using it to solve real problems you already have.
 Think problem first, not tool first. Treat AI like a calculator: reach for it when you hit something it could help with.
 You don’t need to be an AI expert to get value from it. Nobody expects you to “master” a calculator either.
 The easiest way to start: next time you’re procrastinating something, ask AI if it could help.

## The Whole Shebang: [...] Look, you aren’t gonna “learn AI”.

It’s impossible.

It’s too big and it’s a moving target.

You won’t get to the “end”.

It’s not the same as learning, say, how to use Microsoft Word, or Photoshop, where indeed, there are a finite number of tools, setting and skill.

AI is different.

AI is so big and moving so fast there’s no way to “get ahead of it” or “figure it all out”.

But never fear.  That doesn’t mean you’re not gonna learn.

Here’s what you’re gonna do instead:

 You’re gonna learn WITH it.
 You’re gonna be nimble, flexible and embrace experimentation.
 You’re gonna use it to solve real problems.
 You’re gonna learn by doing.

## Instead of trying to “learn AI” as a huge, abstract subject, treat it like a practical tool you use for specific problems. [...] And because AI is so huge, I want to help lower the pressure.

Because, man oh man, is there pressure to “get on the AI train”.

If you are on social media, on LinkedIn, or read the news in any format, you might already feel like you’re behind when it comes to AI.

In Silicon Valley, engineers are starting to be evaluated on how many “tokens” they use.

Companies are going “AI first” (meaning they want their employees to use AI at the start of any project).

And if you’re feeling this pressure, you might be tempted to take a courses on AI, to read books on AI, etc.

But because AI moves so darn fast, by the time you’ve taken the course or read the book, it’s already outdated.

AI has moved on.

The point isn’t to learn AI, it’s to use AI.
